scenario.brief:
**The ticket (ISSUE #1).** There's a typo in the project's README: it says "Invocing" instead of "Invoicing". Fix it.

At Ledgerly, nobody changes the shared code directly. You make your change on your own **branch** (a safe side copy), then open a **pull request** — a polite way of saying "here is my change, please take a look before it goes in." A teammate reviews it, and once they're happy, it gets merged.

**What you'll do.**

1. Get a copy of the repo on your computer (`git clone`), using the link above.
2. Make a branch for your fix: `git switch -c fix/readme-typo`.
3. Fix the typo in `README.md`, save, commit, and push your branch.
4. On GitHub, open a **pull request** into `main`. In the description, write `Closes #1` so it links the ticket.
5. A teammate (**Mira**) will leave a review asking for a small change. Do what she asks, push again, and once she approves, press **Check my work**.

A pull request is a conversation: iterating after review is expected, not a sign of a weak first attempt.
scenario.whyItMatters: This is how almost all professional software changes are made: a branch, a pull request, a review, then merge. Do this once and you understand 90% of daily teamwork on code.

setup: Copy the repo to your computer with the clone command, then open the folder. (Or open it in a Codespace.)
Make a branch for your change so you never work directly on `main`.
Fix the typo in `README.md`, then commit and push your branch.
On GitHub, click **Compare & pull request**, set the base to `main`, and write `Closes #1` in the description.
Wait for Mira's review, make the change she asks for, push again, then come back and press **Check my work**.
commands: git commit -m "docs: fix typo in README"

objectives.title: Make a fix branch
hints: `git switch -c fix/readme-typo` makes the branch and moves you onto it.
The `-c` means 'create'. The name after it is yours to choose; we use fix/readme-typo.
Run it inside the cloned folder.

objectives.title: Commit the typo fix
hints: Open README.md, change 'Invocing' to 'Invoicing', and save.
Then `git add README.md` and `git commit -m "docs: fix typo in README"`.
Push it with `git push -u origin fix/readme-typo`.

objectives.title: Open a pull request
hints: After pushing, GitHub shows a 'Compare & pull request' button. Click it.
Give it a clear title, like 'Fix typo in README'.

objectives.title: Link the ticket
objectives.description: Write 'Closes #1' in the pull request description.
hints: In the PR description box, type `Closes #1`.
GitHub turns `Closes #1` into a link, and closes the ticket automatically when the PR merges.
You can edit the description after opening the PR if you forgot.

objectives.title: Get Mira's approval
hints: Read Mira's review comment and do what it asks (usually a tiny tweak).
Commit and push again — the pull request updates itself, no need to open a new one.
When Mira approves, press 'Check my work'.

debrief.summary: You made a change the professional way: on a branch, through a pull request, reviewed by a teammate, then merged. This is the core loop of working on a team.
internals: A branch let you work without touching the shared main branch.
Pushing put your branch on GitHub so others could see it.
The pull request was the request to merge your branch into main, and the place the review happened.
'Closes #1' linked and will auto-close the ticket when merged.

keyCommands.note: Make and switch to a new branch.
Send your branch to GitHub the first time.
Save your change with a short, clear message.

commonMistakes: Committing straight to main instead of a branch.
Forgetting to push, so the pull request has nothing in it.
Opening a brand-new PR after review instead of just pushing more commits to the same branch.
debrief.atWork: This exact flow — branch, PR, review, merge — is how teams ship code every day. Once it's muscle memory, you're a productive teammate.
debrief.interview: "What is a pull request?" Answer: a request to merge one branch into another, and the place teammates review the change before it lands.
